doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: History of the drumset in Cuban music
summary: How the drumset entered Cuban music and Cuban drummers brought timbales approach to it.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: So you became a drumset player. And you mentioned earlier, when we first started chatting before we were filming that you’re not a percussionist like a hand percussionist, so were you a little out of the ordinary as a drumset player before you came to the States, in Cuba? Don’t some of the — Latin bands don’t always have a drumset player, they sometimes just have a percussion section? Is that correct?

Yeah. Cuban music has gone through different periods. I think the drumset appeared in Cuban music around 1924, 1926, around there. And the drumset appeared in Cuban music because bands, aside of playing Cuban music, they also had to please American and Spaniard tourists. So in order to play fox trots, a famous, a genre from Spain called Paso Dobles that in order to play that date needed a drumset. So that’s when the drums appeared in Cuban music. That was the beginning. But then later on I think I might be wrong, a great Cuban singer, Benny More was the first one who added a drumset or recorded with a drumset. Little by little I cannot talk chronically about the history of the drumset in Cuban music but by the 70s I would say that 80 percent of the bands in Cuba started incorporating drumsets to the band. What happened is that drummers, most of the

drummers in Cuba used to play timbales. So they brought to the drumset the timbales way of playing. So for Cuban drummers from that era we didn’t use timbales, we just used to take the snare off and the snares kind of sounded like timbales and they approach to the music was like if you were playing timbales with three drums and a bass drum. So that’s how the drums started getting in and being part of Cuban music.
